abstract.p: The stemness loss–associated dysregeneration of impaired alveolar type 2 epithelial (AT2) cells abolishes the reversible therapy of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). We here report an inhalable mucus-penetrating lipid nanoparticle (LNP) for codelivering dual mRNAs, promoting realveolarization via restoring AT2 stemness for IPF treatment. Inhalable LNPs were first formulated with dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine and our in-house–made ionizable lipids for high-efficiency pulmonary mucus penetration and codelivery of dual messenger RNAs (mRNAs), encoding cytochrome b5 reductase 3 and bone morphogenetic protein 4, respectively. After being inhaled in a bleomycin model, LNPs reverses the mitochondrial dysfunction through ameliorating nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide biosynthesis, which inhibits the accelerated senescence of AT2 cells. Concurrently, pathological epithelial remodeling and fibroblast activation induced by impaired AT2 cells are terminated, ultimately prompting alveolar regeneration. Our data demonstrated that the mRNA-LNP system exhibited high protein expression in lung epithelial cells, which markedly extricated the alveolar collapse and prolonged the survival of fibrosis mice, providing a clinically viable strategy against IPF.
Inhalable LNPs reprogram alveolar epithelial cells to reverse the stem cell depletion fate against IPF.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) describes a pulmonary disease of chronic and progressive marked by permanent lung function loss and fibrotic remodeling, with a median survival span of 2 to 4 years after diagnosis (1, 2). While existing Food and Drug Administration–approved therapies including nintedanib and pirfenidone have demonstrated therapeutic efficacy in mitigating lung function decline and delaying the physiological progression of IPF, they remain far from achieving IPF revision and both are associated with notable adverse effects (3, 4). Alveolar maintenance and successful regeneration after injury rely on healthy alveolar type 2 epithelial (AT2) cells. Impaired renewal of AT2 cells has emerged as a central factor in the dysregulated alveolar homeostasis that triggers pathological epithelial remodeling and involves the recruitment and activation of fibroblasts, ultimately leading to the accumulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) and distortion of the lung architecture (5, 6). The in-depth studies revealed that AT2 cells play a facultative stem cell role and have the capacity to regenerate injured alveoli by either proliferating or inducting directed differentiation into alveolar type 1 epithelial (AT1) cells (7–9). Considering the pivotal role of AT2 cells in the progression of IPF, maintaining AT2 stem cell identity to facilitate realveolarization is proposed as a promising treatment strategy.

The exhaustion of alveolar stem cells and abnormal activation of multiple pathways related to cellular senescence trigger pulmonary fibrosis, resulting in dysregulation of alveolar epithelium regeneration (10–13). The senescent AT2 cells created an aged-like infamed niche accompanied by loss of stem cell function and accumulation of a stagnant AT2 transitional state, resulting in the pathological remodeling (13–15). Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), which serves as a central factor in energy metabolism, was found to suggest dyshomeostasis in tissues of IPF due to the downregulation of several enzymes regulating NAD+ synthesis, resulting in mitochondrial damage and accelerated cellular senescence (16, 17). Membrane-bound cytochrome b5 reductase 3 (CYB5R3), using reduced form of NAD+ (NADH) as substrate, participates in a variety of redox reactions, affecting lipid metabolism, cholesterol biosynthesis, drug metabolism, oxidative stress, etc. (18, 19). Compared with healthy lungs, the down-regulation of CYB5R3 mRNA and protein levels in IPF lung AT2 cells is not only related to mitochondrial homeostasis associated with the imbalance of NAD+/NADH but also involved in transforming growth factor–β1 (TGF-β1) signaling abnormally activation (20). This suggests that CYB5R3 could be a potential candidate to restore epithelial stem function by resisting accelerated cellular senescence due to mitochondrial damage.

Meanwhile, promoting AT2-to-AT1 cell transition to terminate pathological epithelial remodeling and fibroblast activation is essential for alveolar niche rapid restoration (9). Bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) plays multiple roles in regulating the alveolar niche, which facilitates AT2-to-AT1 differentiation at the expense of proliferation while also restrains fibroblast activation and matrix deposition through signaling in epithelial cells (21–23). In the pathology of pulmonary fibrosis, persistent repression of epithelium BMP4 signaling promotes AT2 aberrant proliferation and fibroblast matrix synthesis, resulting in scarring and alveolar collapse (24, 25). Therefore, we infer that appropriately increasing BMP4 signaling provides a fruitful avenue to maintain the homeostatic relationship between the proliferation and differentiation of AT2 cells for alveolar regeneration as well as inhibiting fibroblast activation.

Messenger RNA (mRNA)–based therapy has emerged as a safe and powerful category of therapeutic modality in various clinical areas such as viral vaccines, protein replacement therapies, genome editing, and cancer immunotherapies (26, 27). However, mRNA-mediated therapies are highly dependent on the optimized delivery vehicles and appropriate administration route (28). Noninvasive aerosol inhalation as a straightforward method has been described as one of the most promising approaches for the treatment of respiratory diseases in clinics due to the unique advantages (29, 30). At the same time, nanoparticle-based delivery systems have been widely applied for lung disease treatments with rapid development of technologies in therapeutics (31–33). Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have been considered as a well-established nonviral nanocarrier for gene therapy with the clinical successes of mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines (34–36). Nebulized LNPs targeting the respiratory epithelium would be ideal for mRNA-based protein replacement therapy in the treatment of IPF because of their preferential accumulation and suitable retention in the lungs (37–39). However, powerful shear forces induced by nebulization and lung-specific barriers, such as mucosal layer and phagocytes, hinder the efficacy of inhaled mRNA therapeutics (40, 41). The challenge of rationally developing and optimizing LNPs for effective delivery of mRNA to the target site remains to be addressed (42, 43).

Recent studies have shown that using lung surface components as nanoparticle surface coatings availably improved spreading over the mucus barrier through interfacial delivery, which has been suggested as a way to shuttle drugs, allowing for better targeting of deep lung tissue and uptake by epithelial cells for drug delivery (44–47). Inspired by this, we proposed incorporating dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC), an abundant phospholipid in pulmonary surfactants, into conventional lipid components to prepare pulmonary surfactant-biomimetic LNPs with mucus permeability for efficient mRNA delivery to lung tissue after being inhaled. In this study, we developed a class of ionizable lipids based on γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) as part of LNP formulations to identify the top lipids and optimized the formulation for high-efficiency mRNA delivery through in vitro screening. Optimized LNPs encapsulated BMP4 and CYB5R3 mRNAs for simultaneous delivery to regulate AT2 stem cell depletion and reconstruct alveolar structure (Fig. 1A). Further work provided that inhaled delivery of mRNA-LNPs markedly reduced lung fibrosis and prolonged survival in a mouse model of bleomycin-induced lung fibrosis.

sec.title: Screening and optimization of inhaled LNPs for mRNA delivery
sec.p: First, we generated an ionizable lipid library by reacting the alkyl tail and amine head with GABA using simple substitution and esterification reactions (Fig. 1B). The structure of ionizable lipids was confirmed by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectra and electrospray ionization mass spectrometry spectra (figs. S1 to S3). To identify stable candidates and formulations, LNPs comprising our in-house–made ionizable lipids—DOPE (1,2-Dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine), DPPC (1,2-dipalmitoyl-rac-glycero-3-phosphocholine), DSPE (1,2-Distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphorylethanolamine)-PEG2000 (polyethylene glycol, molecular weight 2000), and cholesterol—were prepared following an orthogonal design table (Fig. 1C and table S1). Subsequently, we formulated ionizable lipid-based LNPs containing enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) mRNA (EGFP-LNPs) or firefly luciferase mRNA (FLuc-LNPs) for follow-up in vitro screening and in vivo inhalation (Fig. 1D).

We evaluated the mRNA delivery efficiency of these different LNP formulations in murine lung epithelial-12 (MLE12) cells. Notably, GAE14 displayed compatibility with multiple prescriptions and the most substantial transfection potency compared to other ionizable lipid-based LNPs (Fig. 2A). To obtain the optimal formulation of GAE14, we characterized the size, surface charges, mRNA encapsulation efficiency, and stability of five lead candidate formulations (GAE14A, GAE14E, GAE14L, GAE14M, and GAE14N). The results indicated that there was no notable change in the zeta potential before and after nebulization among the five formulations, but the size and polydispersity index (PDI) increased compared to the prenebulized LNP formulations (Fig. 2, B and C). The efficiency of mRNA encapsulation decreased after nebulization due to shear forces, but the GAE14M and GAE14N appeared to better retain mRNA within nebulized LNPs (Fig. 2D). In view of the low difference in the EGFP expression rate of these lead preparations before atomization, we measured the changes in fluorescence intensity of the cells treated with prenebulized and postnebulized LNPs (Fig. 2E). The results showed that GAE14N led to optimal transfection efficiency in epithelial cells. To further investigate the mucus penetration ability of LNPs, we prepared an artificial mucus penetration model (Fig. 2F). These LNPs, at an equivalent dose of carboxyfluorescein (FAM)-mRNA, were added atop the artificial mucus, and a higher fluorescence intensity of the agarose gel layer was detected in the group of GAE14N and GAE14M (Fig. 2G). Considering the transfection efficiency, stability of physicochemical properties, and other factors, we selected the prescription GAE14N to prepare LNPs for subsequent in vivo and in vitro experiments. Both prenebulized and postnebulized LNPs exhibited a small and uniform spherical morphology when examined using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Fig. 2H). TEM histogram revealed that the particle size of LNP before and after nebulization was 80.60 ± 18.41 and 96.08 ± 19.15 nm, respectively (fig. S4A). We then observed that GAE14N LNPs were protected from ribonuclease (RNase) degradation and had high colloidal stability as desirable physical properties, including size, PDI, zeta potential, and encapsulation efficiency, were still observed at 4°C for 8 days (fig. S4, B to E). The uniformity of anti-surfactant protein A (SP-A) antibody-conjugated LNPs (SLNPs) was also confirmed by TEM (fig. S5). In addition, cytotoxicity and expression kinetics were also detected before the efficacy validation experiment. Compared with a previous report (48), LNPs and SLNPs achieved higher cellular viability at the same dose, indicating that LNPs and SLNPs are of great biological safety with negligible toxicity (fig. S6A). Furthermore, we further explored the expression kinetics of SLNP-delivered mRNA. As shown in fig. S6B, bioluminescence was still detected in MLE12 cells over 48 hours after treatment of mRNA-laden SLNPs, and the highest luminescence intensity appeared at 24 hours.

sec.p: We further investigated the uptake of LNPs in MLE12 cells by confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) and flow cytometry assay. The results showed that SP-A antibody-embellished SLNPs significantly improved nanoparticle cellular uptake when compared with the unvarnished LNPs in MLE12 cells (Fig. 2I). Furthermore, to study the effect of different proportions of CYB5R3 and BMP4 mRNAs on alveolar regeneration and repair, primary mouse AT2 cells (fig. S7) separated from lung tissue after intratracheal administration of bleomycin for 9 days. Then, primary AT2 cells were cocultured with mouse lung fibroblasts (MLg2908) embedded in Matrigel medium mix to prepare three-dimensional (3D) organoids models (Fig. 2J). After 10 days of culture, immunofluorescence staining of alveolar organoids showed that the epithelial cells at the periphery of the organoids in the untreated normal group were surfactant protein C (SFTPC)-positive and that those within the interior were aquaporin 5 (AQP5)-positive, which are indicative of AT2-to-AT1 differentiation (Fig. 2K). At a relatively low ratio of mB@SLNPs, the number of AQP5+ AT1 cells increased with the up-regulation of the ratio of mB@SLNPs. However, a high proportion of mB@SLNPs showed an obvious effect of inhibiting AT2 cell proliferation and organoid formation (Fig. 2, L to N). Considering the role of AT2 self-renewal and differentiation potential in alveolar regeneration as well as the experimental results, the preferred ratio of mC@SLNPs to mB@SLNPs was 2:1 (mRNA mass ratio).

sec.title: In vitro abrogation of TGF-β1–induced AT2 cell damage
sec.p: We examined the impact of mRNA-loaded SLNPs on preventing accelerated cell senescence induced by mitochondrial damage in MLE12 cells treated with TGF-β1. Given that AT2 cells from patients with IPF exhibit a marked accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria, the mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) was detected by JC-1 (5,5′,6,6′-Tetrachloro-1,1′,3,3′-tetraethyl-imidacarbocyanineiodide) staining. As shown in Fig. 3 (A and G), the levels of MMP notably elevated as evidenced by the increased ratio of JC-1 aggregates (red)/JC-1 monomers (green) after mC@SLNPs+mB@SLNPs treatment in TGF-β1–induced cells. The dysregulation of mitochondrial function augments oxidative stress, which aggravates lung fibrosis. We then used reactive oxygen species (ROS) probe 2′,7′-dichlorofluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA) and MitoSOX Red reagent to detect intracellular total ROS and mitochondrial superoxide production levels for evaluating the therapeutic effect of combination therapy in reducing ROS production. As depicted in Fig. 3 (B and E), mC@SLNPs+mB@SLNPs could effectively remit oxidative stress compared with the untreated and single-mRNA treatment groups (mC@SLNPs or mB@SLNPs). Meanwhile, as illustrated in Fig. 3 (F and H), strong MitoSOX Red fluorescence was detected in TGF-β1–induced MLE12 cells mRNA, whereas the mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs treatment had a notable inhibitory influence on fluorescence generation. Subsequently, the results of CLSM images (Fig. 3C) showed that mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs significantly improved the expression of cytoskeletal protein vimentin, indicating that dual-mRNA LNPs codelivery had a remarkable effect to reverse AT2 cells damage. To verify if the formulations could reverse cell senescence, the activity of senescence-associated β-galactosidase staining (SA-β-Gal) in AT2 cells was investigated. TGF-β1 stimulation led to a significant rise in the volume of SA-β-Gal+ cells, while the proportion of senescent cells fell in the mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs treatment group (Fig. 3, D and I). Moreover, the Western blot images also demonstrated the down-regulation of BMP4/CYB5R3 protein in TGF-β1–induced MLE12 cells was an obvious amelioration after treatment with mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs (fig. S8). Meanwhile, the level of cellular NAD+ associated with homeostasis was also found to be increased to the baseline level (Fig. 3J). Collectively, these results supported that the mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs group could effectively reverse AT2 cell senescence by alleviating oxidative stress and improving mitochondrial function through increasing the BMP4 and CYB5R3 protein level.

sec.p: To further explore if mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs inhibit fibroblast activation mediated by TGF-β1–induced epithelial cells, we performed transwell experiment to detect the migration capacity of MLg2908 cells. As shown in Fig. 3 (K to M), we found that TGF-β1–induced MLE12 cells could promote fibroblasts migration. However, the opposite effect was observed when TGF-β1–induced MLE12 cells were treated with mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs in the lower chamber, which demonstrated their efficient inhibition effect in fibroblast activation.

sec.title: Therapeutic efficacy of SLNPs in bleomycin-induced lung fibrosis
sec.p: To investigate the biodistribution and mRNA transfection in vivo, we used the Cy5.5-labeled FLuc-mRNA encapsulated in LNPs through inhalation administration to investigate their biodistribution. The in vivo imaging system showed that most of Cy5.5-mRNA@SLNP fluorescence accumulated in the lungs and remained at least 24 hours after nebulization (fig. S9, A to C). A small portion entered the stomach during swallowing. Meanwhile, bioluminescence analysis suggested that LNPs successfully penetrated the lung barrier and effectively mediated mRNA transfection in the lungs (fig. S9, D and E).

We further established a mouse pulmonary fibrosis model in C57BL/6 male mice with a single intratracheal injection of bleomycin to examine the role of different groups on fibrosis treatment in vivo. The experimental scheme with mice is shown in Fig. 4A. From day 9 to day 18 after bleomycin administration, the mice were treated with different preparations via inhalation using a nebulizer every 3 days. Three days after the last dose, the therapeutic effect of repeated inhalation was evaluated. Body weights were recorded every 3 days after initial dosing as a proxy for overall health assessment (fig. S10A). The survival curves (fig. S10B) showed that treatment with mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs significantly extended the survival time of the bleomycin-induced IPF animal model. We used micro–computed tomography (micro-CT) to observe the pulmonary morphological characteristics of mice with pulmonary fibrosis. Ground-glass opacities were identified in the peripheral regions of the lung in the model group (Fig. 4E). By analyzing the 2D micro-CT images and volume of the lung from 3D-reconstituted images, mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs especially showed significant effects in preventing lung lesions and total lung volume reduction (Fig. 4F). After the imaging session, we performed pulmonary function tests (PFTs) to evaluate the impact of different treatments on lung functions in mice. Lung function was impaired in mice after bleomycin injection, but mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs significantly attenuated the decline (Fig. 4, H to M). In particular, the mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs group showed higher dynamic lung compliance, forced vital capacity, inspiratory volume, and tidal volume and lower functional residual capacity and lung resistance compared with the model group and single mB@SLNPs or mC@SLNPs group.

sec.p: To conduct a more comprehensive study of the lung tissue changes in IPF mice treated in different groups, the mice were euthanized and their lung tissues were collected for histological analysis. Homeostasis of the NAD+/NADH ratio in lung tissue suggested restoration of alveolar epithelial mitochondrial function (fig. S11A). We further assessed the concentrations of hydroxyproline in the lungs with a hydroxyproline kit. Treatment with mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs significantly reduced hydroxyproline generation, indicative of reduced collagen deposition (fig. S11B). The difference in collagen accumulation was further confirmed by examining lung sections stained with Masson’s trichrome, which showed a clear decrease in collagen deposition in the mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs-treated group compared with the saline group. (Fig. 4B). Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and picrosirius red staining images of the lung sections found that mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs-treated mice reduced alveolar septum destruction and collagen fiber deposition (Fig. 4B). Consistently, the Ashcroft scale (49, 50) and collagen volume fraction of lung sections confirmed these observations of reduced levels of fibrosis (Fig. 4, C and D). In addition, model mice treated with saline showed significant pulmonary edema marked by an increased lung wet/dry (W/D) ratio while showing a decreased W/D ratio of IPF mice after dual-mRNA combination therapy (Fig. 4G). Overall, these results indicated that mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs treatment reversed bleomycin-induced lung injury and fibrosis, prolonging survival.

sec.title: Alveolar niche remodeling mediated by SLNPs in vivo
sec.p: The alveolar epithelium, composed of AT1 and AT2 cells, is maintained and repaired by the proliferation and differentiation of AT2 cells. The impaired capacity of regenerating alveolar epithelium predisposes to an excessive interstitial fibrotic response. In this study, we investigated the role of BMP4 and CYB5R3 mRNA transmission in promoting the resistance of AT2 cells to damage and their transition to AT1 cells, which is crucial for alveolar epithelial repair. Recent studies have shown that the p53/p21/p16 signaling pathway, associated with AT2 cell senescence, is activated in the lungs of IPF mice, accompanied by increased senescence-associated secretory phenotype–associated gene expression (12, 13). Immunofluorescence assays revealed a significant up-regulation of the senescence marker p16 in the model group treated with normal saline, particularly in SFTPC+ AT2 cells. Instead, treatment with mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs resulted in the down-regulation of p16 expression (fig. S12). Furthermore, examination of alveolar epithelial markers AQP5+ (AT1 cells) and SFTPC+ (AT2 cells) showed a significant decline in bleomycin-injured lungs (Fig. 5, A and B). In contrast, the proportion of both AQP5+ AT1 and SFTPC+ AT2 cells were increased in mB@SLNPs, mC@SLNPs, and mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs (Fig. 5, E and F). Among them, mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs was the most effective therapy. Single-cell suspensions were obtained from digestion of lung tissue for flow cytometry analysis and labeled with markers for epithelial cell [epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM)], AT1 cell [podoplanin (PDPN)], AT2 cell (SFTPC) (fig. S13). Encouragingly, the flow cytometry analysis was further supported by above results (Fig. 5D). Together, these results indicated that mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs support alveolar epithelial differentiation during alveolar repair after bleomycin injury. While alveolar epithelial cells play a pivotal role in driving of pulmonary fibrosis, fibroblasts serve as the direct effector cells of pulmonary fibrosis. During the development of pulmonary fibrosis, the activated myofibroblasts generate large amounts of ECM proteins, resulting in the destroyed alveolar structure. To assess if epithelial repair affects fibroblast activation, we examined the expression of fibrosis indexes [collagen I and α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA)]. It was confirmed that the expression of α-SMA and collagen I significantly reduced in the mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs group by immunohistochemical staining in IPF mouse lung tissue (Fig. 5, C and G to H). Together, these data indicated that the combination of BMP4 and CYB5R3 restores alveolar homeostasis by promoting self-renewal and differentiation of epithelial cells, ultimately reducing collagen accumulation and slowing the fibrotic process.

sec.title: Inflammation remission and biosafety evaluation of SLNPs
sec.p: Last, the inflammatory alleviating ability of mice with pulmonary fibrosis after inhalation administration was evaluated. Bleomycin-induced inflammation led to elevated total protein concentration in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) (Fig. 6A). The profibrotic mediator TGF-β1 and proinflammatory cytokines interleukin-1β (IL-1β), which are involved in the initiation and progression of IPF, were also determined in the collected BALF by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Results showed that mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs treatment significantly inhibited the bleomycin-induced increase of TGF-β1 and IL-1β (Fig. 6, B and C). Giemsa-Wright–stained BALF samples showed significantly increased number of cells in bleomycin induced-mice (Fig. 6, D and E). Decreased counts of inflammatory macrophages and neutrophil were seen following mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs administration (Fig. 6, F and G). Meanwhile, preliminary safety evaluations showed no obvious toxicity by biochemical examination and organ histology. (Fig. 6, H and I, and fig. S14, A and B). In addition, hemolytic assay demonstrated a great biocompatibility of LNPs (fig. S14C).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Clinically, treatments for IPF rely on pirfenidone and nintedanib, which alleviate symptoms and delay lung function decline, but they feebly reverse the fibrosis course and do not significantly extend the median survival time of patients (51). One of the reasons for the failure of existing therapies for IPF is that they focus solely on reducing fibroblast production of ECM, instead of addressing the impaired regeneration of epithelial cells, which is essential for restoring alveolar regeneration in IPF (52). In addition, the presence of mucus barriers impedes the accumulation of drugs in the alveolar space, thereby greatly restricting the therapeutic efficacy of intratracheal administration and inhalation (42). In this study, we designed and established an inhalable dual-mRNA LNP delivery platform, which overcame the mucus layer permeation barrier to achieve deep lung delivery. Our strategy restored the AT2 stem cell niche through rescuing mitochondrial homeostasis and cellular senescence caused by NAD+ metabolic disorders, coupled with a retarded fibroblast activation, ultimately reversing IPF.

The accelerated cellular senescence caused by metabolic disorders and mitochondrial dysfunction leads to either loss or altered function of epithelial stem cells, which promotes dysregulated alveolar repair and pathogenic activation of fibroblasts (8, 11). Recent studies have revealed that the progressive NAD+ diminution promoted mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular senescence in AT2 cells, suggesting a potential way to maintain intracellular NAD+ concentrations for reversing stem cell exhaustion (16, 53, 54). CYB5R3 transfers electrons from the NADH domain to generate NAD+, which is involved in regulating various cellular metabolic processes. The expression of CYB5R3 displayed a marked decrease in AT2 cells from patients with IPF and bleomycin-induced mice, indicating that the up-regulation of CYB5R3 could be a promising therapeutic approach to restore the epithelial stem function (20). While maintaining the stem cell identity, regulating AT2 daughter cell transition and fibroblast activation are also crucial parts to terminate pathologic epithelial remodeling and collagen deposition, ultimately rapidly initiating realveolarization (7, 55). BMP4, a relevant factor that promotes AT2 differentiation and represses fibroblast activation, is diminished after epithelial injury (23, 56). These findings prompted us to consider the synergetic roles of CYB5R3 and BMP4 in antifibrotic responses of restored epithelial cells.

mRNA-based protein replacement therapy is potent yet sensitive and has the potential to revolutionize the way we treat diseases, and LNPs have recently been validated as safe and effective mRNA delivery vehicles (27). Nevertheless, the mRNA-LNP inhaled therapy is still hindered by the impact of shear forces during nebulization and the barrier of lung mucus, indicating a need for further improvement (40, 41). Nanoparticles modified with pulmonary surfactant lipids have been demonstrated to enhance lung barrier infiltration and simultaneously reduce lung tissue clearance (40, 44, 47). In this context, we developed a library of ionizable lipids and incorporated the alveolar surfactant DPPC as one of the lipid components, which were used as a delivery vehicle in the therapeutic mRNA against a bleomycin-induced mouse pulmonary fibrosis model. The optimized formulation exhibits a better mucus penetration and protein expression for inhalation-mediated mRNA delivery to the pulmonary.

Here, we administered LNP-encapsulated CYB5R3 and BMP4 mRNAs separately to epithelial cells and subsequently assessed their capacity for alveolar regeneration through 3D organoid culture experiments. In particular, CYB5R3 maintains AT2 cell homeostasis by regulating NAD+ synthesis to reestablish mitochondrial equilibrium; meanwhile, the BMP4 promotes AT2-to-AT1 differentiation as well as inhibiting the excessive deposition of ECM by suppressing activation of fibroblasts. We found that when codelivering mB@SLNPs with mC@SLNPs at a 1:2 ratio, the balance between AT2 proliferation and differentiation significantly promoted organoid formation. Furthermore, our data demonstrated that the inhaled mRNA LNPs could accumulate effectively and achieve high expression of target protein in the lungs. For in vitro experiments, mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs remised cellular mitochondrial dysfunction and cell senescence. We found that repeated dosing inhalation of LNP treatment attenuated the decline of pulmonary function and prolonged survival in the bleomycin-induced mouse model. Histopathological analysis also demonstrated that LNP treatment substantially attenuated bleomycin-induced alveolar structure collapse, restored alveolar regeneration, and reduced the expression of fibrotic markers (collagen I and α-SMA) and inflammatory cell infiltration.

Although the above delivering strategy shows a considerable therapeutic effect in the bleomycin animal model, the limitation should be noted that a single murine model induced by bleomycin may not reflect all pathologic features of IPF in clinics. The effect of mB@SLNPs+mC@SLNPs on additional animal models and human tissue samples will therefore need to be investigated to further validate the efficacy and repeat inhalation safety. In addition, an improved screening approach, such as high-throughput screening platform in future studies, should be conducted to select LNPs efficiently and sensitively for nebulized delivery.

In conclusion, we developed an inhalable LNP that showed deep lung penetration and cytosolic mRNA delivery to mediate highly effective CYB5R3 and BMP4 translation in AT2 cells. Notably, LNP effectively reversed IPF through resisting depletion of AT2 stem cells as well as abnormal activation of fibroblasts to remodel lung structure. Therefore, our work provides an innovative option for addressing unmet needs in the reversible treatment of IPF by restoring the function of epithelial stem cells to drive alveolar homeostasis and repair.

sec.title: Cell cultures
sec.p: MLg2908 cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 media containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), penicillin (100 U/ml), and streptomycin (100 μg/ml). MLE12 and mouse primary AT2 cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium/F12 medium supplemented with 10% FBS, penicillin (100 U/ml), and streptomycin (100 μg/ml). We used recombinant mouse TGF-β1 (10 ng/ml) to induce damage in MLE12 cells as an injured AT2 cell model for subsequent in vitro studies.

sec.title: mRNA construction
sec.p: mRNAs were transcribed via linearized plasmid encoding codon-optimized murine BMP4 and CYB5R3 and purified in vitro. Briefly, each gene coding sequence was cloned into an in vitro transcription (IVT)-mRNA production template plasmid with a T7 promoter, 5′ untranslated region and 3′ untranslated region elements, and 100 polyadenylate tail. Modified mRNA was generated by full substitution of uridine triphosphate with N1-methylpseudouridine-5′-triphosphate (m1Ψ). 5′ Capping of the IVT-mRNAs was performed cotranscriptionally to obtain the cap1 structure. Last, the purified BMP4 and CYB5R3 mRNAs were verified by capillary electrophoresis and stored frozen at −80°C. The IVT-mRNA sequences are in table S2. BMP4 plasmids, CYB5R3 plasmids, BMP4 mRNA, and CYB5R3 mRNA were purchased from Genscript Biotech Corporation.

sec.title: Preparation and characterization of LNPs and SLNPs
sec.p: LNPs were formulated by pipetting or using the microfluidic device for in vitro screenings and in vivo studies as previously described (57–59). Briefly, an organic phase composed of ionizable lipid, phospholipid, cholesterol, and DSPE-PEG2000 was mixed in ethanol at the molar ratio of different prescriptions (weight ratio of ionizable lipid to mRNA is 10:1). DOPE, cholesterol, and DSPE-PEG2000 were supplied by AVT (Shanghai) Pharmaceutical Tech Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. Ethanol stock solution of ionizable lipid was prepared at 10 mg/ml, and the others were prepared at 5 mg/ml. mRNA (1 μg/μl) was diluted in 50 mM citrate buffer with pH 4.0. Lipid-ethanol solution and mRNA aqueous solution were mixed at the volume ratio of 1:3. Following formulation, resultant LNPs diluted with PBS buffer (pH 7.4) were dialyzed for 2 hours at room temperature using a 10-kDa dialysis cassette and concentrated with a centrifugal filter unit (Molecular Weight Cut-Off, 100 kDa) for in vivo studies. Alternatively, LNPs were diluted with PBS and then filtered through a 0.22-μm filter for in vitro studies.

For SP-A antibody-conjugated LNPs (SLNPs), the above PEG lipids were replaced by DSPE-PEG2000-NHS (N-hydroxysuccinimide) to prepare LNPs by the same method. LNPs containing DSPE-PEG2000-NHS were incubated with SP-A antibody at 4°C overnight in PBS and subsequently were collected and concentrated via centrifugation to remove free antibodies and excess solvent. Antibodies concentration was determined by bicinchoninic acid assay [(BCA) Beyotime Biotechnology].

Fresh LNPs were diluted by RNase-free water or PBS at an mRNA concentration of 1 ng/μl for hydrodynamic diameter, PDI, and zeta potential measurements with dynamic light scattering (Zetasizer ZS90, Malvern Instruments). Then, 5 μl of LNPs was dropped onto specimen grids, and TEM images were collected to observe the morphology of nanoparticles with a transmission electron microscope.

sec.title: mRNA encapsulation efficiency
sec.p: mRNA encapsulation efficiency of LNPs was determined by Quant-iT RiboGreen RNA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a 480-nm excitation wavelength and a 520-nm emission wavelength. Briefly, appropriate LNP preparations were lysed with Triton X-100 and detected with RiboGreen to quantify the total mRNA amount in the sample. Equal amounts of LNPs were directly detected with RiboGreen without Triton X-100 to quantify unencapsulated mRNA. Then, the encapsulation efficiency (in percentages) was calculated as [1 − (mRNA amount in nonlysed LNPs/mRNA amount in lysed LNPs)] × 100.

sec.title: Gel retardation assay
sec.p: LNPs were formulated as described above. Naked FLuc mRNA was included as a control. mRNA LNPs were incubated with RNase (10 ng/ml) at room temperature for 15 min or with 1% Triton X-100 at 37°C for 15 min to verify the protective effect of LNPs on mRNA. Different samples were loaded to a 0.8% agarose gel at 400 ng of mRNA per well, electrophoresed at 120 V for 30 min in tris-acetate-EDTA buffer, and visualized by an imaging system (Amersham Imager 600 RGB, GE Healthcare Life Sciences).

sec.title: Aerosolization of LNPs
sec.p: LNP solution at a final concentration of 0.1 mg/ml of mRNA in sodium acetate buffer (100 × 10−3 M, pH 5.2) was added into the nebulizer unit (Aerogen, Ireland) and nebulized into 1.5 -ml microcentrifuge tubes (prechilled on ice) for in vitro analysis (33, 60, 61). Mice were loaded into a nose-only exposure system that connected to the atomizer. Droplets were added dropwise to the nebulizer (0.5 mg/kg FLuc mRNA, 1 mg/kg BMP4 mRNA, or 2 mg/kg CYB5R3 mRNA), and the mice were removed after aerosolization.

sec.title: In vitro transfection
sec.p: For screening ionizable lipids and optimizing the prescription of LNPs, MLE12 cells were plated in a 96-well or 48-well white-sided plate overnight. LNPs encapsulated with EGFP mRNA were added at 1 μg/ml, and transfection was evaluated via flow cytometry after incubating for 24 hours. CYB5R3 and BMP4 mRNAs were administered in equal or double doses to evaluate efficacy in vitro.

sec.title: Cellular uptake of LNPs
sec.p: MLE12 cells were seeded in confocal dishes (2 × 105 cells) overnight before treatment. Then, PBS, naked FAM-mRNA, FAM-mRNA LNPs, and FAM-mRNA SLNPs were respectively incubated with MLE12 cells for 6 hours. Cells were washed three times with PBS and imaged with CLSM for qualitative analysis and flow cytometry for quantitative analysis.

sec.title: Cellular toxicity of LNPs
sec.p: MLE12 cells were seeded into a 96-well plate (1 × 104 cells per well) overnight. Then, cells were incubated with various concentrations of mC@LNPs or mC@SLNPs (0, 0.175, 0.315, 0.625, 1.25, and 2.5 μg/ml) for 24 hours. Then, the absorbance was measured by a microplate reader (TECAN) at 450 nm after incubation of cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) solution for 1 hour.

sec.title: Intracellular ROS detection
sec.p: The ROS level was detected by the fluorescent probe DCFH-DA. In short, MLE12 cells were inoculated in confocal dishes (NEST Biotechnology) or 12-well plates at a density of 2 × 105 cells/ml overnight. Then, the culture medium was discarded, and various treatment groups were incubated with MLE12 cells for 24 hours. Afterward, DCFH-DA (5 μM) in a serum-free medium was incubated with the cells at 37°C under 5% CO2 for 20 min. After being fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, MLE12 cells were imaged under a confocal laser scanning microscope using the 488-nm laser to detect DCFH-DA. Last, cells were digested, and the content of ROS was analyzed by flow cytometry (CytoFLEX, Beckman).

sec.title: MMP assay
sec.p: The changes in MMP were monitored with the JC-1 probe. Similar to the procedure described above, MLE12 cells were cultured overnight, followed by treatment with different formulations for 24 hours. After washing, cells were incubated with JC-1 fluorescence dye (1×) at 37°C in the dark for 20 min. Images were captured with a confocal microscope, and the fluorescence intensity was quantified using Image J.

sec.title: SA-β cellular senescence assay
sec.p: Cellular senescence was evaluated by an SA-β-Gal staining kit in cells following the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, the cells were fixed with SA-β-Gal staining stationary solution at room temperature for 15 min. After washing three times with PBS, the pre-prepared dyeing working liquid was added and incubated overnight without CO2 at 37°C. The cells were observed and imaged under an inverted fluorescence microscope for the development of blue color on the next day.

sec.title: Artificial mucus construction
sec.p: The artificial mucus was prepared as previously described (62, 63). Briefly, 250 mg of mucin, 500 mg of DNA, 0.295 mg of diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid, 250 μl of sterile egg yolk emulsion, 250 mg of sodium chloride, 110 mg of potassium chloride, and 1 ml of RPMI 1640 were mixed together and suspended with deoxyribonuclease-free water in a final volume of 50 ml. This dispersion was allowed to equilibrate at 25°C for 2 hours. Then, the nanoparticles were placed on the layer of artificial mucus and incubated at 37°C. Undereath the mucus, 10% gelatin gel was present to capture the nanoparticles that penetrated the mucus layer.

sec.title: Transwell assay
sec.p: Migratory capacity of fibroblast cells was investigated with Transwell inserts in 24-well plates (8 μm, Corning). First, MLE12 cells or TGF-β1–induced MLE12 cells (5 × 104, pretreated with different preparations) were added to the lower chamber with 10% FBS media, and MLg2908 fibroblast cells (5 × 104) were seeded in the upper chamber with FBS-free media. After 24 hours of incubation, nonmigrated cells on the upper chamber were removed with cotton swabs, and cells migrated to the lower membrane surface were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and then stained by crystal violet. Five random fields of view were selected under the microscope to count the number of migrating cells.

sec.title: Bleomycin-induced mouse IPF model
sec.p: Five- to 6-week-old male C57BL/6 mice (Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co. Ltd.) were acclimated for 1 week before initiating experiments. All animal procedures were performed in accordance with the Guidelines for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of Shandong University, and experiments were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of the School of Shandong University. The pulmonary fibrosis animal model was established by intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital and a single intratracheal injection of 3 U/kg bleomycin sulfate (Shanghai Yuanye Bio-Technology Co. Ltd) solution. Control mice were administered an equal volume of sterile saline. Nebulizer treatment started with different groups after bleomycin insult for 9 days, once every 3 days.

sec.title: Mouse AT2 isolation and 3D organoid culture
sec.p: Mouse AT2 cells were isolated from C57BL/6 animals and subjected to 3D organoid culture as previously described (64–66). The purity of isolated AT2 cells was typically confirmed by immunofluorescent staining with SFTPC antibody. Primary AT2 cells were mixed with MLg2908 cells and then resuspended into a mixture (1:1) of growth factor reduced Matrigel and organoid medium. After incubating at 37°C for 30 min to allow the matrix to solidify, the culture medium was added to the bottom well and half of it was replaced with warm fresh culture medium every other day.

sec.title: Pulmonary function test
sec.p: Lung function in experimental animals was evaluated with the DSI Buxco-PFT system (Data Sciences International Inc.). After anesthesia, the skin of the neck was dissected and endotracheal intubation was performed. Pulmonary function parameters were recorded to evaluate pulmonary function.

sec.title: BALF collection
sec.p: BALF buffer was obtained with a 1-ml syringe loading PBS by slowly injecting and aspirating three times. Then, the BALF was collected and combined in Eppendorf tubes on ice. After centrifugation, the sublayer cells were stained by Giemsa, and the supernatant was stored at −80°C for cytokine analysis. Then, the cells were stained with modified Giemsa staining solution (Beyotime Biotechnology Co. Ltd).

sec.title: Hydroxyproline assays
sec.p: The hydroxyproline content in the lung was measured by using a hydroxyproline kit (Beijing Solarbio Science & Technology Co. Ltd.), as per manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, the lung tissues were weighed and hydrolyzed in the extract for 2 hours at 100°C until there were no significant clumps. After centrifugation at 16,000 rpm for 20 min at 25°C, the supernatants then underwent a series of chemical reactions. Absorbance was measured at 550 nm using a multifunctional enzyme labeler, and hydroxyproline content (μg) per mg lung tissue was calculated.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Analysis of all data was performed with Student’s t test or ANOVA with Tukey’s followed by multiple comparisons test through a GraphPad Prism software package (Prism 9.0.0, GraphPad Software). The statistical significance of differences for survival analysis was analyzed by the log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test. Significant differences are indicated as ns (not significant), P ≥ 0.05, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, and ****P < 0.0001.
